checks.name: Both directions run
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test cross_language both_directions_agree_across_languages -- --nocapture
checks.output: Observed under bun 1.3.13: '64 value fixtures; rust->bun {"pass":64,"fail":0,"gap":0,"absent":0}; bun->rust {"pass":64,"fail":0,"gap":0,"absent":0}; 7 enum fixtures {"pass":7,"fail":0,"gap":0,"absent":0}; 8 frame fixtures decode {"pass":8,"fail":0,"gap":0,"absent":0}, encode rust->bun {"pass":4,"fail":0,"gap":0,"absent":4}'. The honest breakdown behind those totals: the 64 value fixtures are 60 hex literals (25 accept, 35 reject) plus 4 generator-rule fixtures (2 accept, 2 reject). For the 27 accept fixtures both directions genuinely execute - Rust encodes each one and bun decodes and re-encodes it, and bun hands 25 back as bun_encoded_hex plus 2 as files, all of which the Rust test then decodes and compares. For the 37 reject fixtures there is nothing to encode on either side, so the runner decodes the same bytes once and records that single verdict under both direction keys (conformance/run.ts says so at the call site); the per-direction tally of 64 is therefore 27 real round trips plus 37 single decodes recorded twice. The 8 frame fixtures do not use those two keys: they carry four named checks - input_agreement (bun's rule-built bytes against the ones Rust wrote: 8/8), decode (8/8), encode_rust_to_bun (4/4, 'absent' for the 4 fixtures with no encode clause) and encode_bun_to_rust (4/4) - and 'absent' is tallied separately from 'pass' so an inapplicable check can never be counted as a passing one. The Rust side no longer trusts the runner's exit status alone: it asserts every one of those tallies against the corpus counts, so a runner that silently skipped a section fails the test (negative control 18 confirms this).

checks.name: Byte agreement
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test cross_language both_directions_agree_across_languages -- --nocapture
checks.output: Comparison is byte-for-byte, never structural. Literal fixtures compare hex strings: 25 of 25 identical in the bun-decode direction and 25 of 25 in the Rust-decode direction. Generated fixtures and frames compare raw bytes through files, because a multi-megabyte payload cannot travel as a JSON string this crate's own parser would refuse as over-long: 2 of 2 generated and 4 of 4 encoded frames identical in both directions, including the frame whose payload is exactly 8388608 bytes (8388612 bytes with its prefix). The four-byte big-endian prefix is part of that comparison - writing it little-endian was detected (negative control 11), as was flipping one byte of the frame bun hands back after its own check had passed (control 19) and truncating the generated bytes by one (control 20). The corpus pins the properties that make byte agreement meaningful: key ordering by byte value, exact i64 bounds carried as bigint on the TypeScript side, one spelling per string, and 7 non-canonical spellings refused rather than normalized.

checks.name: Rejection parity
checks.output: 44 rejecting fixtures across the four sections fail in both languages with the same category; comparing every observed_category against the corpus gives zero mismatches. Observed per-category counts, identical on both sides - value fixtures (37): field_invalid 9, malformed_json 7, non_canonical_json 7, invalid_json_value 5, duplicate_key 1, field_grammar 1, integer_out_of_range 1, missing_field 1, nesting_too_deep 1, too_many_entries 1, trailing_data 1, unknown_protocol 1, unsupported_version 1; enum fixtures (3): field_invalid 2, unknown_enum_value 1; frame fixtures (4): empty_frame 2, frame_too_large 2. That is 16 distinct categories, which is exactly the set the TypeScript implementation declares in WIRE_CATEGORIES, so no declared category is unexercised. The runner now also refuses a corpus that names a category it cannot produce (categories_unknown_to_this_implementation was observed empty and the Rust side asserts it), which closes the hole where a typo'd category would have made a rejection fixture unfalsifiable. Rust's own agreement test independently asserts its category equals the corpus for each fixture, so the two implementations are compared against the same declared category rather than against each other.

checks.name: Boundary coverage
checks.output: The corpus now carries length-delimited frames, which it previously had none of. Measured at the declared edges, in both languages: frame-at-max-bytes is a payload of exactly MAX_FRAME_BYTES = 8388608 that both encoders produce identically (8388612 bytes with the prefix) and both decoders accept, reporting consumed 8388612 and payload 8388608; frame-one-past-max-bytes is refused frame_too_large on both paths - from the four-byte prefix 00800001 alone on decode, before any allocation, and from an 8388609-byte payload on encode; frame-zero-length is refused empty_frame on both paths; frame-need-more-prefix asks for 2 more bytes, frame-need-more-payload for 3, and frame-need-more-at-max-bytes for 8388607 without allocating; frame-trailing-bytes-are-not-consumed reports consumed 6 and leaves the next prefix in the buffer. Empty payloads (string-empty, array-empty, object-empty), multibyte UTF-8 at the 2-, 3- and 4-byte boundaries in one string, nesting at exactly MAX_NESTING_DEPTH = 32 and one past it, and the exact i64 ceiling and floor with a one-past rejection were already present and still pass. Newly added at their exact and over-limit bound: the JSON string ceiling (65536 accepted, 65537 refused field_invalid), the container entry ceiling (4096 accepted, 4097 refused too_many_entries), the protocol name (64 / 65), the request identifier (128 / 129), the message kind (64 / 65), the retained read-only enum spelling (64 / 65), and the empty spelling of each bounded field. Payloads too large to review as a hex literal are generator rules in the corpus (the largest literal is 219 bytes); both implementations build the bytes from the rule and the runner compares its bytes against the ones Rust wrote before any verdict is believed - a rule read one byte differently was detected (negative control 17). RESIDUAL GAP, stated rather than papered over: the contract's fixture-contract paragraph also asks for every R1-02 primitive at its exact and over-limit bound. The bounded-text rule shared by OpaqueId and BoundedString is covered above in its wire-visible form, and EpochMillis is covered by the i64 bounds, but PublicHttpUrl, SecretText and Revision still have no wire representation in this slice and none was invented for them, because R1-06 adds no protocol semantics; covering them needs a schema mapping that does not exist yet.

checks.name: Compatibility tolerance
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test cross_language && cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test wire
checks.output: All three clauses are now driven through the real decoders in both languages. Unknown additive fields: envelope-unknown-additive-field carries a future_field inside the body, is accepted and byte-identical in both languages, and a new Rust test asserts the field survives the round trip rather than being dropped. Unknown security-sensitive values: enum-security-unknown carries decision 'allow_always' and both languages observed the refusal category unknown_enum_value, while enum-security-known observed 'known:allow'; TypeScript gained decodeSecurityEnum, whose return type is the union of defined spellings, so a caller cannot receive one this build does not understand. Unknown read-only values: enum-read-only-unknown-value observed 'unknown:hibernated' in both languages - the same spelling, preserved, not defaulted - enum-read-only-known observed 'known:running', enum-read-only-unknown-at-max-bytes observed 'unknown:' followed by 64 x characters, and the 65-byte and empty spellings were refused field_invalid in both. These fixtures reach Rust's decode_security_enum, decode_read_only_enum and ReadOnly::Unknown, which the old harness never invoked, and the mirrored TypeScript decoders. The corpus declares each enum's kind, field and known spellings, and a test asserts that declaration equals the Rust definition, so the two cannot drift (negative control 7 confirms the assertion bites). Negative controls 3, 4, 12 and 13 confirm that dropping the read-only bound or letting an undefined security-sensitive spelling through is detected in both languages.

checks.name: Negotiation coverage
checks.command: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test cross_language && cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p automonique-protocol --offline --test wire envelope_admission
checks.output: The structural gap is closed: Message::from_canonical_bytes_admitted now consults a declared protocol set, mirrored by decodeMessageAdmitted in TypeScript, and the harness drives every envelope fixture through it against the set the corpus declares (automonique.runner 1..=1 and the 64-byte boundary name 1..=1). Two new fixtures were observed refused identically in both languages: envelope-unknown-protocol, a well-formed envelope naming automonique.unimplemented, refused unknown_protocol; envelope-unsupported-major, naming automonique.runner at version 2, refused unsupported_version. The two axes stay distinct and neither is downgraded into the other - collapsing them was detected (negative control 6). Shape is settled before negotiation: seven Rust tests in tests/wire.rs cover admission, including four payloads that are both malformed and name an unimplemented protocol, each of which is refused with its shape category (missing_field, field_grammar, field_invalid, non_canonical_json) rather than unknown_protocol, and an empty supported set which implements nothing and admits nothing. Two genuine cross-language divergences were found and fixed on the TypeScript side while wiring this up, with fixtures added to pin them: an empty or control-bearing protocol, request_id or kind was reported field_grammar by TypeScript and field_invalid by Rust, because TypeScript judged the grammar before the shared bounded-value rules; and a version outside u32 was reported field_invalid by TypeScript and invalid_json_value by Rust. Rust is the source of truth, so TypeScript was changed to its order and its categories (negative controls 15 and 16 confirm both fixes are load-bearing).

checks.name: Offline execution
checks.command: strace -f -qq -e trace=%network -o net.trace rust/target/debug/deps/cross_language-<hash> --test-threads=1 ; env -i PATH=<empty dir> rust/target/debug/deps/cross_language-<hash> both_directions_agree_across_languages --nocapture
checks.output: Measured, not argued. Tracing every network syscall of the whole test binary, which forks bun, produced a 504-line trace containing zero socket, connect, bind, listen, sendto or recvfrom calls of any family: all 504 lines are SIGCHLD and SIGPWR signal notifications from bun's threads. No daemon is started and no Unix socket is read; the runner's only import is node:fs plus a relative module, and the new file exchange writes into a per-process directory under the system temp dir. The missing-runtime path was exercised, not assumed: with PATH pointing at an empty directory the test printed 'GAP: no JavaScript runtime; cross-language conformance is unmeasured' and wrote an artifact containing "measured":false with a reason, having first written all 16 Rust-side exchange artifacts. Recorded as a caveat, unchanged from the previous audit: in that state the cargo test itself still reports ok, so a green suite alone does not prove the cross-language claim was measured - the gap is visible only in stderr and the artifact. The Rust side does now assert "measured":true whenever a runtime was found, so a runner that reported an unmeasured run while one was available would fail.

notes: Three rows that were failing are now closed and the fourth, Quality, is re-measured green at this base. What changed: the corpus gained length-delimited frame fixtures at the exact ceiling, one byte over, zero length and both incomplete-frame edges, expressed as generator rules so an 8 MiB payload does not become an unreviewable literal; TypeScript gained the frame codec, the read-only and security-sensitive enum decoders, the shared bounded-value rules and protocol admission, all mirroring the Rust already landed by R1-02 and R1-03; and Message::from_canonical_bytes_admitted wires SupportedProtocol::admit into the envelope decode path so a well-formed envelope naming an unimplemented protocol can be refused at all. No protocol semantics were invented: every rule the TypeScript side gained already existed in Rust, and the two enums the enum fixtures drive are declared in the test file, not in the crate. Two real cross-language divergences were found while doing this and fixed in TypeScript, since Rust is the wire source of truth: bounded-value rules must precede field grammars, and a version outside u32 is invalid_json_value rather than field_invalid. One gap remains and is recorded under Boundary coverage rather than hidden: PublicHttpUrl, SecretText and Revision have no wire representation in this slice, so the fixture-contract clause asking for every R1-02 primitive at its exact and over-limit bound is only covered for the primitives that do appear on the wire. Two smaller scope choices, stated so a reviewer need not infer them: sdk/typescript/packages/protocol/src/index.ts was left alone, so the new frame, enum and admission surface is reachable from src/canonical.ts but is not re-exported from the package entry point; and conformance/node-runtime.d.ts gained two local declarations (a binary readFileSync/writeFileSync overload and Bun.version) because the file exchange needs them, which is inside this item's allowed paths but outside the file list it was handed.
